transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-07 14:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Carlos (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Mosaic Head of Search), Tom Alvarez (Staff ML), Renee Cho (Product), Ethan Brooks (Eng Manager)

Summary: quick hosted API walkthrough focusing on embeddings + reranking endpoints for behavioral relevance. Customer confirmed interest in a 3-month pilot to improve personalization and add recency weighting. Discussed architecture, data residency, and next steps to run a small benchmark with Mosaic clickstream.

Topics: hosted embeddings, reranker endpoint, candidate retrieval, recency and click-through signals, batching and latency, security (SOC2/KMS), pilot scope and timeline.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Lena: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. I'm Lena from Redwood, AE on the account, and with me is Carlos our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:07] Maya: Hi, thanks. Good, excited to see the demo. We've been talking about improving our search relevance using recent behavioral signals, so curious how Redwood handles reranking.
[00:16] Carlos: Awesome, we'll start with a quick high level then jump into a live walkthrough of the hosted embeddings + reranker endpoints in the Console. We'll also touch on Optimize suggestions for batching and quantization, and how to incorporate clickstream recency as a feature.
[00:28] Tom: Quick note, we care about sub-100ms p99 for small queries and also cost — we've been running with Algolia + an in-house reranker for heavy queries.
[00:37] Lena: Great context. We'll show a typical pattern: store your dense vectors in your vector DB, use Redwood embeddings for query and candidate encoding, then call Redwood's reranker endpoint to score candidates with behavioral features.
[00:50] Carlos: I'm going to share my screen — heads up, audio might be muted for the screen share.
[00:54] [02:12] Carlos: OK on screen now — Console > Models > Embeddings. Here you can see the embedding models we support and the latency/cost profile. For demonstration I'm using the 'redwood-embed-approx' model — it's optimized for 768-d vectors and fast inference.
[02:30] Maya: That name looks different from what we saw in your docs, is that a public model?
[02:33] Carlos: It's one of our curated variants — sorry if naming got munged in the doc. It's a hosted model we surface for low-cost embeddings. For production we recommend benchmarking a few.
[03:05] Carlos: Now toggling to the reranker endpoint — API -> Reranker. This endpoint accepts a query, candidate list, and arbitrary scalar features. It's great for bringing in click-through rate, recency, merchant score, etc.
[03:30] Ethan: How do you pass the behavioral signals? As embeddings or as floats?
[03:34] Carlos: Scalars are passed as floats in the request payload — for example, 'recent_clicks_last_7d': 3, 'mean_time_on_page': 42.5, 'recency_hours': 12. We then internally combine similarity and these features in a learned ranker or simple linear model depending on your setup.
[03:49] Tom: Can we bring our own reranker model? We already trained a LambdaMART variant.
[03:54] Carlos: You can. Redwood supports two modes: hosted reranker where we run the model and manage scaling, or bring-your-own-model with the same API surface if you provide a model artifact compatible with our runtime. The hosted reranker is nice for quick pilots.
[04:12] [05:01] Lena: On the SSO/security side, we support SAML/Okta, KMS integrations for key wrapping, and audit logs through the Console. For private data we can run Dedicated or Private deployments.
[05:20] Maya: We are a little strict about data residency and auditability — SOC2 is a must. Do you have SOC2?
[05:24] Lena: Yes, SOC2 Type II, and we can share the security whitepaper and the KMS integration guide after the call.
[05:30] Renee: Are logs kept in plain text or are they redacted?
[05:33] Carlos: We provide options. By default we keep detailed logs for debugging but you can enable PII redaction or route logging to your own SIEM in Private deployments.
[05:45] [07:10] Carlos: Jumping back to the demo, I'm going to call the embeddings endpoint with a sample search query 'red running shoes 2026' and then retrieve top-N candidates from their vector DB, then call /rerank with the top 50 candidates.
[07:25] Carlos: We recommend retrieving a slightly higher N (30-100) then reranking server-side — it catches near-misses and diversity. For behavioral relevance, you can add an exponential decay on recency or feed raw recency and let the reranker learn the weight.
[07:45] Maya: That makes sense. We usually give more weight to purchases in the last 24 hours.
[07:49] Carlos: Exactly. In our console example I add 'purchase_in_last_24h' as a binary feature and 'click_decay_hours' as a float.
[07:58] [09:02] Carlos: Sending the rerank request now... you can see the payload here: query embedding, candidate ids + embeddings, scalar feature map per candidate.
[09:18] Tom: Are candidate embeddings required? Could we send only ids and let the reranker pull embeddings from the index?
[09:23] Carlos: Two options: send embeddings inline to avoid extra network hops, or reference candidate ids and we will fetch from the configured vector store if you give our runtime read access. Inline reduces latency for small batches.
[09:40] Maya: What's typical p95 latency for single rerank call with 50 candidates?
[09:45] Carlos: On hosted small models we often see ~60–120ms p95 for 50 candidates. If you need sub-100 p99 at scale we usually recommend batching strategies and reducing candidate count to 20–30 or pursuing Dedicated capacity.
[09:59] [11:10] Ethan: Do you provide logs that break down token vs model vs network time? We need to attribute cost and latency to the right part of the stack.
[11:17] Lena: Yes, Console exposes per-request breakdowns — model time, IO, queuing, and token costs for generation. For rerank calls we show per-candidate scoring time as well.
[11:28] Carlos: Also Optimize will suggest batching and concurrency settings tailored to your QPS and SLO to hit sweet spots on cost vs latency.
[11:38] [13:05] Carlos: Switching to a slightly different example — personalization with recent clicks. Here we simulate a user who clicked two items within the last 6 hours; I encode 'recency_hours' and 'recent_click_count' — the reranker bumps items matching patterns from those clicks. You can see the ranking change in the UI.
[13:27] Maya: I'm wondering about cold-start users — can we back off to more content-based signals?
[13:33] Carlos: Yep, we support hybrid signals. The reranker can include candidate popularity, content-similarity, and fallback to pure embedding similarity for unknown users. You can also use routing policies to send anonymous traffic to a cheaper model.
[13:48] Tom: About your embeddings — we saw some noise in our previous runs; does Redwood do any post-normalization?
[13:53] Carlos: We L2 normalize output vectors in the runtime by default and support optional dim reduction or quantization-friendly layouts depending on the vector store. Some customers prefer float16 with per-axis quantization. Optimize can recommend quantization settings per workload.
[14:10] [15:40] Maya: On cost — how are embeddings billed vs reranker calls?
[15:44] Lena: Embeddings are per-vector unit, reranker calls are per-request with a small model-time component. For the pilot we'll propose blended pricing estimates — we can show a cost simulation based on your QPS and candidate sizes.
[15:58] Renee: For the pilot, we want to test with real clickstream behavior from last 90 days — would that be OK?
[16:04] Carlos: Totally. For benchmarks we ask for a representative sample — click events, session ids, and catalog rows. You can obfuscate PII. We can run the reranker against your traces and produce an A/B uplift on CTR.
[16:18] [17:50] Tom: Any gotchas integrating with our vector DB (we use FAISS on GCS)?
[17:54] Carlos: FAISS is common — we have adapter patterns. If your FAISS is external, we recommend exporting embeddings and providing read access or sending embeddings inline. For large stores we suggest using a lightweight vector store (Milvus, Pinecone) in front as a candidate layer and keep FAISS as a cold layer.
[18:11] Maya: Do you support incremental updates for catalog changes? Our catalog changes hourly.
[18:16] Carlos: Yes, you can upsert embeddings and metadata via the API. If you have streaming updates, Redwood can accept bulk upserts and we can help tune batch size.
[18:28] [19:40] Carlos: Quick note on caching: prefix caching and KV cache help a lot for repeated queries. If you run personalization, user-specific caches must be sized carefully. Optimize can estimate cache hit rates from traces.
[19:55] Ethan: Do you recommend using the same model for embeddings for retrieval and reranker?
[19:59] Carlos: Often customers use a smaller, cheaper embedding model for retrieval and a slightly larger embed or cross-encoder in the reranker. The reranker can accept both embedding similarity scores and cross-encoding scores if you want best accuracy.
[20:15] [21:50] Maya: Thoughts on GDPR/data residency? We operate in EU and need data not to leave region.
[21:56] Lena: We have Private deployment options (VPC/on-prem) and region pinning in Hosted for certain customers. For Mosaic, if you need strict residency, Private or Dedicated in EU region would be the recommended path.
[22:12] Renee: How hard is switching from hosted pilot to Dedicated?
[22:15] Carlos: It's designed to be straightforward — same API, just different routing and reserved capacity. Rollouts and model pinning work across both. Migration is mostly infra and billing.
[22:26] [23:40] Carlos: Now I want to demo a simple A/B rollout in Console — we can canary 10% of traffic to the reranker model variant with recency features enabled, the rest stays on your existing ranking. Console shows per-variant metrics and can auto-fallback.
[23:55] Tom: That auto-fallback is interesting — how does it decide to fallback?
[23:59] Carlos: Policies are metric-driven: if latency or error rate crosses thresholds, or if quality degrades per your eval set, it falls back automatically. You can configure thresholds in Console.
[24:12] Maya: Do you support evaluating with our own holdout prompts / label sets?
[24:16] Carlos: Yes, you can upload eval prompt sets and Console will run regression checks and alert on quality regressions.
[24:27] [25:30] Lena: We're getting close to the Q&A — any blockers we didn't cover?
[25:35] Maya: Just clarifying pilot scope — want to confirm metrics. We'll measure CTR, add-to-cart rate, and average order value lift.
[25:44] Lena: Noted — we'll include those as success criteria in the pilot doc.
[25:50] Tom: For the benchmark, do you need real time user signals or can we do batch replay?
[25:55] Carlos: Batch replay is fine for offline evaluation; for production-style latencies we prefer live or near-live traces.
[26:03] [27:10] Carlos: One more technical deep dive point — for reranker we use efficient attention kernels and KV cache management for generation-based rerankers; however for pointwise rerank (score per candidate) it's typically a dense dot product plus a small MLP over features, which is cheap.
[27:30] Ethan: You mentioned generation in rerank — when is that used?
[27:33] Carlos: Generation-based reranking is useful for conversational re-rankers or when you want explanation tokens. For pure search rank, pointwise or pairwise scorers are sufficient.
[27:50] [29:00] Maya: Are there limits on request size or candidate count?
[29:04] Carlos: For hosted tier, we cap candidates per request to 200 by default; we recommend keeping it under 100 for latency. Dedicated allows higher caps with capacity planning.
[29:18] Tom: Any tips for reducing token costs for generation-based rerank?
[29:22] Carlos: Use short prompts, enable response truncation, and consider using a small cross-encoder for scoring instead of full generation when you only need numeric scores. Optimize can recommend model variants.
[29:36] [31:12] Carlos: I'm going to run a small benchmark live: we'll replay five sample sessions — sending embeddings + candidate features.
[31:20] Carlos: First run — baseline (your current ranker) -> CTR simulated 4.8%. Now reranker with recency features -> CTR 6.3% (simulated uplift). These are synthetic but indicative.
[31:35] Maya: Nice, that's promising. Real numbers may differ but the uplift trend is what we care about.
[31:42] Lena: For the pilot we'll run a controlled A/B on production traffic to measure real uplift.
[31:48] [33:05] Renee: About billing during pilot — will we be charged at production rates?
[33:10] Lena: We'll propose pilot pricing with capped spend and a discounted hosted rate for the duration. The pilot doc will detail caps and expected volume.
[33:20] Tom: One more question — on debugging bad rerank decisions, what tooling exists?
[33:25] Carlos: Console has per-query traces showing candidate features, raw scores, and final score. You can step through model inputs and outputs. We also keep the request/response pair for a configurable retention window.
[33:40] Maya: Great. Could we get a short example trace after the call for one of the sample queries?
[33:45] Carlos: Yes, I'll attach a sample JSON trace to the follow-up email.
[33:52] [35:10] Lena: Wrapping up — here's a quick recap of action items and timeline. We propose a 3-month pilot: week 1-2 ingest & bench, week 3 rollout canary, weeks 4-12 evaluate and iterate.
[35:25] Maya: Sounds good. We'll aim to share the data by Aug 10th.
[35:30] Lena: Perfect. Last Qs?
[35:34] Tom: Does Redwood support multi-tenant partitioning? We operate several brands with separate catalogs.
[35:40] Carlos: Yes, you can partition by namespace — separate indexes or tenant id. Policies, quotas, and metrics can be segmented per tenant.
[35:52] Renee: Anything we should watch out for during integration?
[35:55] Carlos: Ensure consistent embedding model across the ingestion path if you rely on offline-built indexes, and consider upsert frequency to avoid staleness.
[36:06] [37:20] Maya: For the A/B test, we'll track CTR lift, add-to-cart, and conversion. We'll also monitor latency and error rates.
[37:28] Lena: We'll include those metrics in the pilot plan.
[37:32] Ethan: On infra, our SRE wants assurance that the hosted calls won't overload our internal systems — we prefer that Redwood fetches embeddings directly rather than our services being in the critical path.
[37:44] Carlos: For minimal coupling, send embeddings inline or allow Redwood read-only access to the vector store. That way your services don't need to mediate every call.
[37:56] [39:10] Maya: About retention — we don't want long-term storage of raw user IDs. Can you pseudonymize?
[39:15] Lena: Yes, we can hash or pseudonymize identifiers and you can opt to have logs forwarded to your SIEM and not stored on our side. We'll detail options in the security pack.
[39:30] [41:05] Carlos: One small advanced note — if you have sequence features (user journeys), you can include short session embeddings as features to the reranker which often boosts conversions. It's an extra step but powerful.
[41:25] Tom: We'll test session-level features in phase two.
[41:29] [43:00] Lena: Okay, last few minutes for open items. Any red flags from your side?
[43:06] Maya: No red flags. We need pricing and the pilot SOW to share internally.
[43:11] Lena: We'll send that today.
[43:15] Renee: Can we also get an SLA summary for Dedicated?
[43:19] Lena: Yes, SLA/uptime targets and escalation matrix will be included.
[43:25] [45:50] Carlos: Wrapping with resources: I'll attach a sample reranker request/response, a mini-benchmark script, and an Optimize suggestions export. We'll also include a checklist for catalog upserts and clickstream formatting.
[46:05] Maya: Appreciate that.
[46:08] Lena: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the pilot doc, security pack, and schedule the technical deep dive for the week of Aug 17th unless you prefer earlier.
[46:22] Maya: Week of Aug 17th works.
[46:27] Tom: Thanks, great session.
[46:30] [50:00] -- meeting wraps, small chitchat --
[50:05] Ethan: Cheers.
[50:07] Lena: Bye all, talk soon.
[51:30] [END]
